Route turns with Brisk-S and the few-shot prompt: it is the only one of the 9 configurations inside all three gates, at $1,200.00 a month.

It reaches 90.7% balanced accuracy, its whole interval above the gate, and holds every cell floor. What could change the call is latency: its p95 of 184 ms has no interval, so a production measurement above 250 ms would leave no configuration standing.

!
Confidence: High, if the caveats below aren't material.
  • Latency budget (p95) is cleared on a point estimate. only if Brisk-S few-shot's true p95 is more than 66 ms slower than measured: then it misses the budget and no configuration passes every gate.
  • The pick is the best of several candidates. only if a fresh run reads Brisk-S few-shot's balanced accuracy more than 0.7 points lower, or its Complex × News cell more than 2.9 points lower; as the one passer of 9, its figures read somewhat high.
  • No arm is the control. only for claims that one configuration beats another; the call reads each configuration against fixed gates, not against a control.
RecommendationShip Brisk-S with the few-shot prompt on all turns. It clears overall balanced accuracy at 90.4–91%, every one of the nine cell floors, and the latency budget at 184 ms.
Why not the othersEvery Atlas-M prompt and Brisk-S with the rubric prompt miss the latency budget (Brisk-S rubric at 496 ms). Nano-XS few-shot clears latency and, on its point estimate, overall accuracy, but misses the Complex × News cell at 76.7%, clear below the floor. The zero-shot prompts and Nano-XS rubric miss accuracy.
WatchThe thinnest margin is overall accuracy: 0.7 points above the gate, interval 90.4–91%, and above 90.7% nothing passes. Complex × News is 2.9 points above its floor; in noise the two are about equally safe, each more than twice its half-width. Latency headroom of 66 ms rests on a point estimate.
NextMeasure Brisk-S few-shot's p95 latency with an interval under production load; it is the one gate the call cannot yet show it clears beyond noise.

Two configurations clear both the latency budget and the overall accuracy gate, Brisk-S and Nano-XS with the few-shot prompt; every Atlas-M prompt and the Brisk-S rubric fall out on latency, the rest on accuracy.

The Latency (p95) axis is on a log scale: its values span more than ten times.

Balanced accuracy against p95 latency (log axis), with the gates at 90% and 250 ms; Nano-XS few-shot's overall interval, 89.8–90.4%, straddles its gate.

The cell floor separates the two: at Complex × News, the weakest cell for both, Brisk-S few-shot clears the floor by 2.9 points, while Nano-XS few-shot fails there and nowhere else.

Accuracy in each complexity × domain cell, with its interval and count; the floor is 80%.

On Brisk-S, few-shot examples lift balanced accuracy by +4.7 points and the rubric prompt adds only +0.8 more while breaking the latency budget; the prompt's effect depends on the model, and the rubric costs Nano-XS accuracy against few-shot.

Each model × prompt tile: balanced accuracy, cost per 1,000 turns, p95 latency and whether it passes every gate. Few-shot gains more on Nano-XS than on Atlas-M by +9.6 points.

Next steps

  • Measure Brisk-S few-shot's p95 latency, with an interval, under production load. Whether the pick clears the latency budget beyond noise; if not, no configuration passes and the budget or the model needs a decision.
  • Add Complex × News examples to the Nano-XS few-shot prompt and re-run that cell and the overall set. Whether Nano-XS few-shot becomes eligible; the monthly cost gap to Brisk-S few-shot is +$1,143.00. Nano-XS must also clear the overall gate on its interval, today 89.8–90.4%.
  • Run Brisk-S few-shot on a fresh holdout of about 19383 turns, the size at which four runs in five confirm the overall clearance if today's figure is the truth. Whether the pick's thin overall clearance survives outside the set it was chosen on.

Left out, and why

Traffic-weighted accuracy and macro F1
Neither is gated, and both rank the configurations as balanced accuracy does; they don't change the call.
Confusion tables on complexity and domain
Each axis on its own reads well for both few-shot configurations; they don't locate the Complex × News loss, which is a joint error.
The full lever and interaction table
Prompt and model interact clearly (c3 cites the largest interaction), but the call rests on gates read per configuration, not on averaged effects; the full table stays in the appendix.
Atlas-M rubric's top accuracy
It is out on latency by a wide margin, so its accuracy doesn't bear on the call.
Failure examples
No failed turns were kept for review in this campaign.

Method

Cases
48210 labelled turns per configuration, each run once, spread over nine complexity × domain cells.
Accuracy
The share of a cell's turns given the correct label, with an interval per cell at the level the cells state, uncorrected.
Balanced accuracy
The plain mean of the nine cell accuracies; its interval is derived from the cells' intervals, read as independent.
Gates
Balanced accuracy at least 90%, each cell at least 80%, p95 latency at most 250 ms; all three declared before the run, each read on the point estimate.
Latency
p95 only, with no interval stated.

Caveats: Latency budget (p95) is cleared on a point estimate.

Cost
Dollars per million turns, priced at 30000000 turns a month.
Comparisons
No control; prompt and model effects compare two configurations' own intervals as if independent, so they read wide.
Source
Synthetic example data from docs/eval-report-kit/references/r3-classifier.json

Review findings left open

  • Should fix · The page: The latency budget row in What you could change says the call holds for any budget at or above 184 ms. That is right: the sweep keeps Brisk-S few-shot as the pick at every higher budget, because it is the cheapest passer. But at 483 ms Atlas-M few-shot also passes all gates (92.1%, $0.26 per 1,000 turns), and at 496 ms so does Brisk-S rubric (91.5%, $0.095). From those points the headline's 'only one inside all three gates' no longer holds, and the pick rests on cost. Add a clause such as: 'from 483 ms, Atlas-M few-shot also passes at +1.4 points and 6.5× the cost; the pick then rests on cost.' A reader weighing a looser budget for more accuracy would then see the trade.
  • Should fix · The page: In the second next step, 'the monthly cost gap to Brisk-S few-shot is +$1,143.00' doesn't say which way the gap runs. Nano-XS few-shot costs $57 a month against $1,200 for Brisk-S few-shot. Say plainly that Nano-XS few-shot would save about $1,143 a month. The cell-floor row could also say that below 76.7%, Nano-XS few-shot would become the pick only on a point estimate: its overall interval, 89.8–90.4%, straddles the 90% gate.
